fact: Fender began using the large headstock logo and a new serial system starting with "S6." 1976 coincided with America's Bicentennial—some Strats featured a special 'Bicentennial' neck plate.
CBS-era Fenders now used plastic 'F' tuners, a controversial update among purists.
Many late-70s Fenders featured a 3-bolt neck plate for easier setup, a divisive feature that returned to 4-bolt in later years.
This year marked the last before most Fender US production moved to Corona. Many late-70s models are known for thick polyester finishes.
Fender's US factory at Fullerton produced millions of instruments in the '70s, but quality debates raged. The iconic 'bullet' truss rod and large headstock became Strat mainstays.
Major artists like David Gilmour and Nile Rodgers defined the Fender sound in the late '70s, with 'Black Strat' and disco-funk Telecasters heard on countless records.
Fender launched the American Vintage Reissue Series, meticulously recreating the '57 and '62 Stratocasters.
CBS sold Fender to its employees, marking the birth of modern 'Fender Musical Instruments Corporation.'
The American Standard Stratocaster returned, featuring a new 2-point tremolo and modern electronics.
Lace Sensor pickups began appearing in Strat Plus and Ultra models, giving players a quieter, high-tech tone.
Fender's US E-series models saw reissues of classic '50s models and modernized features, restoring Fender's reputation.
Eric Clapton's 'Blackie' Strat and Jeff Beck's 'Hot Rod' models made the '80s a defining era for signature Fender sounds.
After a fire in Corona, Fender's Ensenada, Mexico factory began full-scale production—ushering in affordable, quality MIM models.
Fender's 50th Anniversary year saw special edition guitars and commemorative badges.
The American Deluxe Series debuted, introducing noiseless pickups and rolled fingerboards.
The last year for N-series US serials before the Z-series began in 2000.
MIM Fenders ('Made in Mexico') brought Strat and Tele models to a new generation—artists like John Frusciante and Billie Joe Armstrong embraced them on stage.
The 'American Standard' defined US Fender quality through the '90s, while 'Squier' models surged in popularity among new players.
S-1 switching system debuted on American Series Strats, adding versatile tone options.
Fender introduced 'Delta Tone' circuitry, letting Strat players bypass the tone circuit for a hotter bridge sound.
Fender's 60th Anniversary was marked by special badges and commemorative diamond inlays on select models.
Fender upgraded fretwork and neck finishes for better playability across American and Mexican models.
The Z-series era brought new consistency and premium hardware to American and Mexican Fenders. Player favorites: American Deluxe Strat, Player Series Tele, and Highway One models.
Artists like John Mayer, H.E.R., and Jim Root brought new signature Fenders to the spotlight in the 2000s and 2010s.
American Standard Strats and Teles got custom-shop Fat '50s pickups, giving a more vintage-correct sound.
Fender launched the American Elite Series, featuring compound-radius fingerboards and fourth-generation noiseless pickups.
The Player Series replaced the long-running Standard Series in Mexico, introducing Alnico pickups and fresh finishes.
COVID-19 lockdowns drove a record surge in new players; Fender Play signups soared as many picked up guitar for the first time.
American Professional and Player Series Fenders raised the bar for consistency and playability, earning praise from hobbyists and artists alike.
Artists like Vulfpeck, H.E.R., and Ed O'Brien (Radiohead) pushed new sounds on modern Fenders, proving the classics never go out of style.
